question: How well can one aggregate calibrated experts' posterior means without knowing their joint information structure, assuming their latent signals have diminishing informational returns?

key_findings.claim: The paper supplies a clean robust-aggregation model that compares one report-only rule with the posterior available to an omniscient observer of every expert signal.
key_findings.evidence: Each expert reports Yi=E[Y|sigma_i]. Quality is reduction in squared error relative to the prior, v(X), and performance is v(X)/v(Y_[k]). The adversary may choose any square-integrable information structure satisfying the stated substitutes restriction.

key_findings.claim: Weak submodularity of signal value is insufficient: a secret-sharing construction makes every report uninformative most of the time while the set-value function remains additive.
key_findings.evidence: Randomizing a Shamir threshold r gives v(Y_A)=|A|/k, hence weak substitutes, but all expert posterior means equal the prior unless r=1. Thus no report-only rule, even with the prior, beats the random-expert 1/k approximation on that structure.

key_findings.claim: Projective substitutes is a mathematically meaningful strengthening that controls cross-prediction, not merely the marginal value of signal sets.
key_findings.evidence: For every A,B,i it requires the squared error with which A predicts B's posterior not to increase when i is revealed to both sides. Via conditional expectation as Hilbert-space projection, this is equivalent to full revelation being dominant in the paper's team-scoring mechanism.

key_findings.claim: Without the prior, simple averaging guarantees about 1.866/k of omniscient improvement, and no rule can uniformly exceed 2/k-1/k^2 over the class.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 combines an exact bias-diversity identity, projective cross-prediction inequality, weak submodularity, and Pythagorean projection. The Gaussian unknown-location family supplies the upper bound through minimax estimation of its mean; for two experts the 0.706 positive bound is exactly tight.

key_findings.claim: Knowing the exact prior makes fixed-factor linear extremization provably better in the same worst-case sense.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed rule multiplies the average experts' displacement from E[Y] by a k-dependent d tending to sqrt(3), guaranteeing about 2.598/k. For two experts its approximately 0.760 guarantee is tight over all aggregation strategies, not only linear rules.

key_findings.claim: The headline constant-factor gains still imply a worst-case guarantee that vanishes as the expert count grows.
key_findings.evidence: Both positive bounds are Theta(1/k), so under the allowed adversarial information structures adding experts can make the guaranteed fraction of omniscient value arbitrarily small. The results are relative improvement ratios, not bounds on absolute squared error or a claim that averaging becomes more accurate with k.

key_findings.claim: Projective substitutes is latent, target- and loss-dependent, and not operationally testable from the inputs given to the aggregator.
key_findings.evidence: Checking Definition 2.8 requires the joint state/signal distribution and conditional posteriors for every subset A,B and expert i, while deployment provides only one vector of posterior means (and perhaps the prior). The paper gives a small table example and Gaussian families but no observable diagnostic, statistical test, or broad characterization of real forecasting ensembles satisfying it.

key_findings.claim: The formal setting assumes ideal Bayesian truthful experts and excludes the central reliability problems of real forecast pools.
key_findings.evidence: Yi is exactly E[Y|sigma_i], reports are noiseless real numbers, every expert shares squared-error objectives, and no one is strategic, adversarial, biased, miscalibrated, rounded, missing, or distribution-shifted. Equal weighting also ignores known skill differences and provenance duplication.

key_findings.claim: The recommendation to extremize by a universal factor should not be transferred directly to probability forecasts or other losses.
key_findings.evidence: The Hilbert projection proofs require real-valued posterior means and squared loss. Linear extremization may leave a bounded outcome domain, and clipping changes the theorem. The paper explicitly distinguishes its setting from probabilistic aggregation and leaves nonlinear extremization open.

anchors.section: Robust aggregation and extremization related work

key_findings.claim: Later work exposes complementary ways to trade worst-case ignorance for computation, samples, richer reports, calibration, or narrower structure classes.
key_findings.evidence: NeurIPS 2023 studies learning an aggregator from outcome-labeled samples; algorithmic robust aggregation computes near-minimax rules for specified families; second-order reports help only under additional restrictions; 2026 work treats unknown priors/state spaces and output calibration. These directions address information and implementability gaps rather than dominating the projective-substitutes theorem.

method.core_idea: Restrict adversarial Bayesian information structures through a new cross-projection diminishing-returns property, then optimize worst-case squared-error improvement using only experts' posterior means and optionally the prior.
method.mechanism: Conditional expectations are represented as orthogonal projections in L2. A bias-diversity identity decomposes the error of the mean into individual posterior errors minus pairwise disagreement. Projective substitutes lower-bounds useful disagreement, while submodularity telescopes residual information. Carefully optimized inequalities yield averaging and extremization constants; indistinguishable finite structures and Gaussian minimax estimation yield lower bounds.
assumptions: Experts truthfully report exact Bayesian conditional means from a common information structure.
The target and every forecast are square-integrable real-valued random variables.
Performance is squared-error improvement over the exact prior.
The latent information structure satisfies projective substitutes for all signal subsets.
The aggregator receives a single report vector and, in one setting, the exact prior mean.
The all-signals posterior is the appropriate omniscient benchmark.
Worst-case approximation ratio, rather than absolute risk or data-driven average performance, is the objective.

techniques.role: Strengthens submodular signal value into cross-posterior prediction monotonicity.
Turns Bayesian posterior relations into squared-distance geometry.
Expresses average-forecast error using expert errors and pairwise disagreement.
Normalizes an aggregate's gain over the prior by omniscient posterior gain.
Uses known prior to amplify the average update by an optimized constant.
Upper-bounds any prior-free rule using unknown-mean estimation.
Separates weak from projective informational substitutes.

evaluations.setting: Prior-free aggregation over all projective-substitutes structures with k experts
evaluations.metric: Worst-case fraction of squared-error improvement achieved by the all-signals posterior
evaluations.result: Averaging guarantees at least (1+sqrt(3)/2)/k-O(1/k^2); no rule uniformly exceeds 2/k-1/k^2, and the stated positive constant is tight for k=2.
evaluations.baseline: Uniformly selecting one expert, guaranteed 1/k under weak substitutes.

evaluations.setting: Known-prior aggregation over the same class
evaluations.result: A k-dependent linear extremization factor tending to sqrt(3) guarantees 3sqrt(3)/(2k)-O(1/k^2); the approximately 0.760 two-expert result is tight over all rules.
evaluations.baseline: Unextremized average and all prior-free aggregation strategies.

evaluations.setting: Analytic counterexample families: Shamir thresholds, unknown-mean independent Gaussians, fully dependent Gaussians, and paired finite two-expert structures
evaluations.result: The constructions establish impossibility under weak substitutes, a general prior-free upper bound, a fixed-extremization upper bound, and exact two-expert lower bounds.

limitations: Projective substitutes cannot be verified from a single observed report vector.
The condition depends on the target, squared loss, and the full latent information structure.
All experts are exactly Bayesian, truthful, calibrated, and square-integrable.
Only real-valued point forecasts and squared loss are covered.
The all-signals posterior observes raw signals unavailable to a report-only aggregator.
Guarantees decay as Theta(1/k), and no absolute-risk guarantee is provided.
Bounds remain non-matching for general k in the prior-free setting.
Known-prior optimality for arbitrary nonlinear rules remains open beyond two experts.
There is no empirical evaluation or test of the assumption on real forecast pools.
Skill heterogeneity, malicious reports, rounding, missingness, repeated questions, and shift are omitted.
failure_modes: Complementary signals such as XOR or threshold secret sharing make individual posterior means hide joint information.
A pool that violates projective substitutes has no stated performance guarantee.
Unknown location/prior makes individually sensible reports insufficient to reconstruct the aggregate target.
Universal extremization overreacts when reports are highly redundant and underreacts when evidence is independent.
Linear extremization can output an infeasible probability or bounded physical quantity.
Miscalibrated or strategic experts invalidate the conditional-expectation projection identities.
Duplicated models or shared training data can cause equal weighting to overcount one information source.
A ratio can be unstable or undefined when the omniscient posterior adds negligible value over the prior.
Large k can leave a formally improved but operationally tiny worst-case guarantee.
reusable_insights: Distinguish submodularity of information value from substitutability of observable posterior reports.
Use posterior disagreement as useful signal only after proving that disagreement relates to missing information.
State whether an aggregation guarantee concerns absolute risk, regret, or a fraction of oracle improvement.
Treat knowledge of the prior as substantive side information, not a harmless normalization.
Test robustness claims against indistinguishable latent structures that demand conflicting actions.
Before extremizing, model redundancy and verify output-domain constraints.
Pair structural minimax guarantees with sample-based calibration and assumption diagnostics.
open_questions: Is there an observable or sample-efficient test for approximate projective substitutes?
Which common generative graphical models imply projective substitutes under squared loss?
What are the exact optimal ratios and rules for k greater than two?
Can nonlinear known-prior aggregation uniformly beat fixed-factor extremization?
How do guarantees change for bounded outcomes, clipping, log loss, or general proper scores?
Can one tolerate approximate calibration, biased reports, adversarial experts, or strategic disclosure?
Can historical forecast-outcome samples interpolate between structural robustness and learned aggregation?
Can output calibration and Blackwell refinement be imposed without losing robust approximation guarantees?

competitive_landscape.title: Informational Substitutes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational substitutes framework used by the paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen and Waggoner define value-function notions including weak substitutes and study optimization/information aggregation consequences. Neyman and Roughgarden show that set-function submodularity is too weak for report-only robust forecasting and introduce cross-projection substitutes.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust Forecast Aggregation
competitive_landscape.difference: Arieli, Babichenko, and Smorodinsky minimize regret for binary probability forecasts under two-expert Blackwell ordering or conditional independence. This paper handles arbitrary k and real targets but assumes projective substitutes and uses an improvement ratio instead of regret.

competitive_landscape.title: From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Alternative max-min aggregation foundation by the same authors.
competitive_landscape.difference: That work derives quasi-arithmetic pooling from proper scoring rules, axioms, and subcontracting incentives and supports learning weights across rounds. The reviewed paper instead derives equal averaging/extremization from adversarial latent information structure under squared loss.
competitive_landscape.source_version: current arXiv record / Operations Research version

competitive_landscape.title: Sample Complexity of Forecast Aggregation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later data-driven alternative to structural worst-case aggregation.
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin and Chen assume outcome-labeled samples from the unknown report distribution and quantify learning an approximately optimal aggregator, finding exponential expert dependence generally but dimension-free rates under conditional independence. The reviewed rule is zero-sample but conditionally robust.

competitive_landscape.title: Algorithmic Robust Forecast Aggregation
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo et al. compute approximate minimax aggregators for finite families and restricted two-agent conditional-independence models. This trades the reviewed paper's closed-form rule over a broad axiom class for explicit computation over a specified uncertainty set.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust Decision Aggregation with Second-order Information
competitive_landscape.difference: Pan, Chen, and Kong ask whether predictions about other experts' recommendations improve binary decisions. They show no general benefit but gains under conditional independence/homogeneity, illustrating another way that observable side information needs structural restrictions.

competitive_landscape.title: Prior-Agnostic Robust Forecast Aggregation
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen, Peng, and Tang allow unknown binary state values and derive closed-form log-odds pooling with near-tight minimax regret for conditional-independence, Blackwell-ordered, and general regimes. It addresses prior ignorance and bounded probabilities under different structural assumptions and metric.

competitive_landscape.title: Algorithmic Expert Aggregation
competitive_landscape.difference: Tang and Zhang require the output itself to remain calibrated and seek Blackwell refinements identifiable from reduced-form input experts, proving efficient randomized algorithms and deterministic hardness. The reviewed paper optimizes squared loss but does not guarantee aggregate calibration.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Projective substitutes identifies a broad robust-aggregation regime where averaging beats a random expert and known-prior extremization is provably better still.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The secret-sharing separation, cross-projection definition, sharp two-expert bounds, and closed-form constants are substantive theoretical contributions. Earlier robust aggregation treated narrower binary/two-expert structures, and prior informational-substitutes work did not yield these report-only guarantees. The scope is nevertheless narrower in practice than 'broad' suggests because the condition is latent and ideal Bayesian assumptions are strong.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is high as information-economics theory and moderate as actionable forecast methodology. The most durable contribution is showing exactly what stronger property is needed beyond submodular signal value; the extremization factor is a minimax certificate within that model, not a universal empirical recipe.

reviewer_notes: Read all 25 extracted pages, including every definition and theorem, the complete positive proofs, secret-sharing and Gaussian lower bounds, exact two-expert constructions, known-prior derivation, references, and omitted-proof appendix. Audited benchmark semantics, ratio asymptotics, observability of assumptions, domain/loss transfer, calibration, and deployment gaps. Competitors were checked in primary arXiv and OpenReview/NeurIPS records through 2026-08-23.
